newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Malta, Spain, stopovers for key Rwanda arms plane.
newsitem.headline: Malta, Spain, stopovers for key Rwanda arms plane.

text.p: Two years after the genocide in Rwanda, a U.N. commission is trying to uncover the activities of a former Rwandan army colonel who ordered weapons for exiled Hutus in complicity with Zairean officials, according to a new U.N. report on Tuesday.

One such shipment was in May 1994, a month after the massacres had begun against minority Rwandan Tutsis. In the armed conflict that followed, defeated Hutu forces were setting up bases in or near Zaire, according to a U.N. Commission of Inquiry investigating arms into the region.

The commission said a Nigerian-registered B707 aircraft left Madrid for Malta on May 24, 1994, and went to eastern Zaire, apparently carrying 30 tonnes of arms. The colonel, Theoneste Bagosera, was believed to have boarded the plane in Malta.

The commission has not yet received a reply from the Spanish government but Malta said it had carried out its own investigation. It said the aircraft was not bound for Goma, Zaire, but for Lagos, Nigeria and that no passenger by the name of "Bagosera, T." could be traced from the immigration records.
But the commission wrote again to the Maltese government and said a declaration submitted by the crew of the aircraft names Bagosera. It asked the government to check again.

"On October 4, 1996, the chairman of the commission wrote again to the Maltese government making reference to the general declaration submitted by the crew of the aircraft in question, which named 'Bagosera, T.' as the passenger, and requesting the government for further documentary evidence," the report said.

Bagosara has been accused of playing a central role in the 1994 genocide that killed about one million Rwandan Tutsis and of trying to re-arm the exile resistance to the Tutsi-led force that became the present Rwanda government.
He is now in jail in Cameroon after Belgium requested his detention and extradition on charges that he killed 10 Belgian soldiers based in Rwanda as U.N. peacekeepers in April 1994.
The commission in a report in March said Bagosera operated from Zaire, where resistance to the Tutsi-led force that eventually took power in the summer of 1994 is still centred.
The scheme uncovered in 1994 showed weapons were bought by Bagosera with the help of a South African, Willem Ehlers, a private citizen believed to have brokered the transactions.

The weapons were picked up in June 1994 in the Seychelles, where the government has since barred further shipments. At that time the commission established that rifles, mortar shells and ammunition were flown aboard an Air Zaire DC-8 cargo plane from the Seychelles, islands on the east African coast, to Goma.

The commission in its new report was attempting to trace the origin of weapons, middlemen out for profit or companies used in transport of arms through a number of European countries including Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, France, Britain, Italy and Belgium. Aside from Zaire, the Hutu rebels set up military training camps in Tanzania and raised funds and organised the ventures through Kenya, the report said.
